text.p: Holderbank , the world's biggest cement producer, on Monday said 1996 results would at best only reach 1995 levels because of weak European economies and poor construction weather earlier this year.

Chairman Thomas Schmidheiny said recession in Europe -- Holderbank's biggest market -- was compounded by a harsh winter across much of the continent at the start of this year that stalled construction.
"At best, group results for 1996 will reach the level of the year before," Schmidheiny told a news conference on half-year results.
"However, thanks to a solid performance in North and Latin America, the shortfall against last year's results should be kept within limits," he added.
Schmidheiny said his 1996 forecast referred to Holderbank's share of post-tax net excluding minority interests.
Holderbank reported a 1995 group net profit of 629 million Swiss francs ($506 million) for 1995, on group net sales of 8.27 billion francs.
In the first six months of 1996, the Swiss-based maker of cement and other building materials said consolidated net income after taxes fell 7.5 percent to 283 million Swiss francs.
After deducting minority shareholder's interests, Holderbank's share of net income totaled 217 million Swiss francs, a drop of 8.0 percent or 19 million.
It said that sale of non-strategic assets raised additional ordinary income by 92 million Swiss francs to 128 million.
Consolidated net sales rose 13.8 percent, or 543 million Swiss francs, to 4.481 billion -- due mainly to major acquisitions led by the Swiss-based Societe Suisse de Ciment Portland.

By region, net sales totalled 2.32 billion Swiss francs in Europe, 788 million in North America, 808 million in Latin America and 674 million in Asia, Oceania and Africa, less 109 million for sales between business units.

Changes due to its scope of consolidation generated 567 million Swiss francs, along with 18 million gained on currency translation effects. Concurrently, price and volume fluctuations reduced turnover by 42 million.
Schmidheiny said setbacks suffered by the majority of European units due to bad weather were hardly likely to be made good by the end of this year.
"Europe's contribution to the 1996 consolidated results is thus expected to be a disappointing one, falling short of budget expectations," he said.
In contrast, North America looked positive and Latin American business was also growing.

"Poised for a solid financial performance over the year as a whole, Latin America will, along with North America, once again be a mainstay of the group as whole in 1996," he said. ($1=1.2427 Swiss Franc)
